method_card.title: Quadratic nth Term, Functions and Iteration
steps: Quadratic sequence: halve the second difference for a, subtract an² to find bn + c.
f(x): replace x with the input. fg(x): do g first, then f.
Inverse f⁻¹: swap x and y, then make y the subject.
Iteration: put xₙ into the formula to get xₙ₊₁; repeat.
method_card.content:
A quadratic sequence has a constant second difference \(d_2\). Its nth term is \(an^2 + bn + c\) with \(a = d_2/2\). Subtract \(an^2\) from each term, then find the nth term of the linear remainder for \(b\) and \(c\).

Functions: \(f(3)\) substitutes \(x = 3\). Composite \(fg(x)\) applies \(g\) first, then \(f\). The inverse \(f^{-1}(x)\) reverses \(f\): swap \(x\) and \(y\), then rearrange.

Iteration: \(x_{n+1} = g(x_n)\) turns one approximation into the next; repeat until the digits stop changing.
method_card.example:
Find the nth term of 3, 9, 19, 33, 51

Second difference 4, so \(a = 2\). Subtract \(2n^2\): 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Remainder 1.

Answer: \(2n^2 + 1\)

bronze.display: A quadratic sequence has second difference 6. What is the coefficient of \(n^2\)?

misconceptions.message: The coefficient of \(n^2\) is HALF the second difference: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Using 6 itself skips the halving.

bronze.hint: The coefficient of n squared is half the second difference.

guided_steps.say: The number in front of \(n^2\) is always half the second difference.
guided_steps.hint: It is given in the question.

guided_steps.done: Doubling returns the second difference, so a = 3 is right.

steps.say: That steady growth of the jump, always 2, is the second difference. When it stays constant the sequence is quadratic: its nth term has an \(n^2\). Halve the second difference for the number in front of \(n^2\) (here \(2 \div 2 = 1\)), and these really are \(n^2 + n\): 2, 6, 12, 20.
\(f(5)\) means put \(x = 5\) into \(4x - 1\). Read the input first.

steps.say: A full quadratic nth term. First the second difference.

steps.pre: Halve it for the n² coefficient: 4 ÷ 2 =
steps.hint: a is the second difference divided by 2.

steps.say: Now subtract \(2n^2\) from each term to leave a linear sequence.
The remainder 3, 4, 5, ... rises by 1, giving \(n + 2\). So the nth term is \(2n^2 + n + 2\).
steps.done: Matches the sequence, so the nth term is 2n² + n + 2.

bronze.title: Bronze: put one value in
steps: Function notation \(f(x)\) is a machine: whatever sits in the brackets replaces every \(x\). \(f(4)\) means swap \(x\) for 4, then work it out.
For a sequence, the second difference is the difference of the first differences. A constant one means the sequence is quadratic.
Take care squaring negatives: \((-3)^2 = 9\), never \(-9\) or \(-6\).

silver.title: Silver: two linked steps
steps: Composite \(fg(x)\) works inside out: do \(g\) first, then put its answer into \(f\). Order matters, so \(fg\) and \(gf\) usually differ.
An inverse \(f^{-1}(x)\) undoes \(f\). Write \(y = f(x)\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), then make \(y\) the subject.
An iteration formula feeds each answer back in: find \(x_1\), then reuse it to reach \(x_2\).

gold.title: Gold: the full method
steps: For a quadratic nth term, halve the second difference to get \(a\), then subtract \(an^2\) from every term to leave a linear sequence.
Find the nth term of that leftover (constant difference \(b\)); the result is \(an^2 + bn + c\).
To solve \(fg(x) = k\), build the composite, set it equal to \(k\), and solve. To iterate to a root, repeat the formula until the digits settle.
